scorecard.rationale: Three independent randomized human trials outside Parkinson disease report lower visual-analogue pain with encapsulated oral cinnamon bark powder versus starch placebo in primary dysmenorrhea (n=114, 24-72 h), migraine (n=43 completers, p<.001), and rheumatoid arthritis (n=36, abstract p<.001), alongside a high-attrition multiple-sclerosis trial with baseline imbalance and endpoint switch (VAS vs registered PQAS). Competing controlled trials show null upper abdominal pain for cinnamon-sesame macerate versus sesame oil and inconsistent exercise-soreness findings, while the single Parkinson rehabilitation case combined cassia with multimodal therapy. One oral ground Ceylon cinnamon experiment in female rats found smaller bladder-distension reflexes with induced cystitis and larger responses in uninflamed bladders at the same higher dose. The mixed animal proxy supplies no transferable sign. Differences in culinary ground exposure, non-Parkinson pain etiologies, and reporting limits keep the favorable easing signal at minimal_signal. An identified Cinnamomum burmannii extract in a cellular screen supplies preparation context without a pain-severity or Parkinson observation. Cinnamon is an identification odor in the acute-illness comparison. The paper has no assigned culinary cinnamon pain treatment or attributable pain contrast. The review lists cinnamon as one source of eugenol. Isolated-eugenol trials have chemical, thermal and motor results in rodents, with controlled human oral cinnamon evidence still the closest basis.
